findings.claim: Landon's “Captain Cook (To My Brother)” is read as a poem about family separated by distance: “Landon presents belonging as something that can stretch across distance”; “Even as Cook sailed to the other side of the world, the idea of home and family remained a… anchor”; “nature is the medium through which separated people remain connected — they look at the same sky, are carried by the same wind”; Key Fact “The sea and sky connect brother and sister even when they are apart.”
findings.truth: The siblings are never apart in the poem. Landon recalls that her brother brought home Cook's Voyages one August evening and that they played the book out together in their garden: “the pond amid the willows the ocean seem'd to be” and “The water-lilies… We call'd the South Sea islands”. The loss is time, not distance: “we both of us are alter'd”, “There is not of that garden a single tree or flower; / They have plough'd its long green grasses”. No shared sky or wind appears anywhere in the poem.
findings.evidence: Full text at https://revisionworld.com/level-revision/english-literature-gcse-level/poetry/pre-1914-poems/captain-cook-my-brother-letitia ; Oak National Academy lesson notes (garden destroyed = siblings' bond broken) https://www.thenational.academy/teachers/programmes/english-secondary-ks4-edexcel/units/poetry-anthology-first-study-203/lessons/analysing-the-poem-captain-cook-to-my-brother

findings.claim: KC[3] “Landon uses the natural imagery of the sea and sky to present nature as a _____ connecting separated family members”, keyed to “bridge”; KC[4] match pairs Landon with “Connects — nature bridges distance between people”.
findings.truth: Same error as F1 in the answer key. The garden is a shared, present place the children turn into an imagined ocean; nobody is separated by distance. Questions and keyed answers rewritten to the poem's real content.

findings.claim: “That belonging can stretch across physical separation — nature becomes the bridge between separated people”; “Landon uses nature as a connecting thread between distant people”; “adventure, departure and family bonds”.
findings.truth: Same error as F1 carried into the memorisation cards. Rewritten to the shared childhood game and its loss.

findings.claim: PQ[1] mark scheme: “sea/sky imagery as connecting separated siblings… Age of exploration, family separation.”
findings.truth: Same error as F1 in the mark scheme, so a correct answer would be marked down. Context is the popularity of Cook's Voyages as reading in 1820s British homes, not the poet's family being separated by voyaging.
findings.evidence: Poem text (see F1 URL); Landon 1802–1838, Cook died 1779.

findings.claim: KC[1]: “Why is the communal 'we' voice significant in Clare's 'The Sunday Dip'?”, and PQ[1] mark scheme rewards “communal 'we' voice”.
findings.truth: “The Sunday Dip” has no first-person plural at all. It is third person throughout: “The morning road is thronged with merry boys… They run to seek the shallow pit… The boldest ventures first and dashes in… And play about the water half the day.” A student who knew the poem would be marked wrong by this key.

findings.claim: “boys swimming in a stream on Sundays”; “a flowing, narrative structure that mirrors the movement of the stream” (repeated in lesson 6: “a village stream is the centre of communal life”).
findings.truth: There is no stream in the poem. The boys “seek the shallow pit” and paddle under willow trees. The form is rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter, not a loose narrative flow.

findings.claim: “For Brontë, belonging is not about people or buildings — it is about being absorbed into the natural world.”
findings.truth: The poem's turn is exactly the opposite: the mist takes the speaker back to a family home. “Oh, I'm gone back to the days of youth, / I am a child once more, / And 'neath my father's sheltering roof / And near the old hall door”.

findings.claim: “Brontë uses a series of natural images — mist, cloud, wind”.
findings.truth: There is no wind in the poem. Its images are mist, cloud, rain, damp grass and scent.

findings.claim: Zephaniah “was a diasporic poet — his parents came to Britain from Jamaica”.
findings.truth: Zephaniah was born in Handsworth, Birmingham, to a Barbadian postman and a Jamaican nurse. Only his mother came from Jamaica.

findings.claim: “Chingonyi was born in Zambia but raised in England after both his parents died” (repeated in PQ[4] mark scheme and flashcard 11).
findings.truth: Chingonyi moved to the UK aged six, in 1993, after his father died — his mother was alive and was studying in Britain. She died when he was thirteen. He was not orphaned before the move.

findings.claim: Key Fact quotes “sound of the sea” as a phrase from “Island Man”.
findings.truth: That phrase is not in the poem. The line is “to the sound of blue surf / in his head”. A student quoting “sound of the sea” would be quoting text that does not exist.

findings.claim: PQ[5] mark scheme: “the single-word final line 'Another London day'”.
findings.truth: The final line is three words. It is isolated on its own line, which is the real structural point.

findings.claim: KC[1]: “Why does Zephaniah use the collective 'We' rather than 'I' or 'They'?”, and lesson text “Zephaniah uses the collective 'We,' making the poem a communal statement.”
findings.truth: The poem is built on first-person singular stanzas — “I come from a musical place”, “I come from a beautiful place” — alternating with the refrains “We can all be refugees” and “We all came from refugees”. The question's premise that he avoids “I” is false.

findings.claim: “Kunial explores the gap between his father's Kashmiri heritage and his own English upbringing” and “His poetry often inhabits the space between two languages — English and Urdu — and 'Us' makes this linguistic borderland visible.”
findings.truth: Neither Kashmir, nor his father, nor Urdu appears in “Us”. The poem's language material is inside English: “maybe it's a Midlands thing / but when I was young, us equally meant me”; football supporters “cresting the Mexican wave of we or us”; “my heart's sunk at separations of us”. His Kashmiri-English heritage is legitimate context, but the lesson presents it as the poem's content.

findings.claim: “The Belonging anthology includes poems written in free verse, sonnets, dialect, and standard English”; section heading “Traditional Forms: Sonnets & Regular Metre”; description “…free verse and sonnet form”; lesson 7 PQ[3] mark scheme “free verse vs sonnet”.
findings.truth: The Belonging collection contains no sonnet. Its 15 poems use rhyming couplets (Clare, Landon), ballad-type quatrains (Wordsworth, Brontë), twelve-line stanzas (Bridges), eight-line stanzas (Hood), tercets (Kunial) and free verse (the rest). The sonnet in the anthology (Barrett Browning's Sonnet 43) is in the Relationships collection, not Belonging.
findings.evidence: Spec Appendix 3, specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1905–2250 (Belonging and Relationships lists).

findings.claim: Banned strings present in five lessons: “Component 2” (L1 exam tip, L7 content, L7 flashcard) and an AO code followed by a full stop, “AO3.” (L1 content, L6 content, L8 content, L8 conclusion).
findings.truth: scripts/_validate_content_json.py rejects the whole unit on /\bComponent\s+[0-9]/i and /\bAO[1-4]\./ across description, content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html and practice/knowledge-check text. Seven occurrences rewritten to house phrasing.

findings.claim: “Bridges (writing around 1900)”.
findings.truth: “Clear and Gentle Stream” was published in The Shorter Poems of Robert Bridges, 1890.

findings.claim: “the adjective 'mild' to personify the mist as gentle and unthreatening” (repeated in PQ[2] mark scheme, flashcard 2 and the lesson 8 quotation bank).
findings.truth: Defensible but weak. “Mild” is a normal weather adjective; the poem's unmistakable personification is elsewhere — “the day has wept its fill, / Spent its store of silent sorrow” and “As thick as morning's tears”. Teachers commonly accept “mild” as personification, so no edit; but the stronger evidence is missing from the quotation bank.

findings.claim: “Zaffar Kunial — born 1981.” (also “Zaffar Kunial (born 1981)” in content_html).
findings.truth: No public source gives Kunial's birth year — Wikipedia, the Poetry Foundation, Faber and the Scottish Poetry Library all omit it. The date cannot be verified, so it should probably be dropped rather than corrected.

findings.claim: Every practice question in all eight lessons carries type “20 marks — Poetry Comparison” or “4 marks — Quote Analysis”, including questions whose own text says [10 marks] and single-poem questions that are not comparisons.
findings.truth: The type labels do not match the questions. Left unedited because the retro programme already runs a separate question-type relabel workstream (190 items); editing here would collide with it.
findings.evidence: e.g. L1 PQ[1] text ends “[10 marks]” but type is “20 marks — Poetry Comparison”.

findings.claim: Clare's “language is simple and direct, rooted in the dialect and rhythms of rural England”, and “sensory detail… the cold water, the splashing”.
findings.truth: “The Sunday Dip” contains no dialect words and never mentions cold water. The sensory detail it does have is “the thunder in their ears” and the rush boat under the willows. Loose rather than false, so no edit.

summary: Every exam claim in the unit matches the spec (20 marks, AO2 15 + AO3 5, named poem printed, closed book, unseen comparison assessed on AO1 and AO2) and the 15-poem collection list is correct with no invented poets. The damage is in three poems: Landon's “Captain Cook (To My Brother)” is misread throughout lesson 2 as a poem about family separated by distance when it is about a shared childhood game in a garden; Clare's “The Sunday Dip” is credited with a communal ‘we’ voice it does not have; and Kunial's “Us” is credited with Kashmiri and Urdu material it does not contain. Two biographies (Zephaniah's parents, Chingonyi's orphaning) are wrong, one quotation is fabricated, the collection is said to contain a sonnet it does not, and seven banned strings would fail the house validator.
